222	
223	## 5. What the revival changed in Fortress itself
224	
225	Changes a programmer writing Fortress would notice, by area.
226	
227	### Numbers
228	
229	- The number types are siblings under `Number`, not a tower, as the team's compiler library already had them. A wider type converts from a narrower one by a declared `coerce`.
230	- Fixed-width overflow raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk, as on the compiled path. To wrap on purpose, write ∔, ∸ or ⨰.
231	- An integer power answers its base's type. A negative exponent raises an error, except at the bases 1 and -1. For a fraction, write `2.0^(-1)`.
232	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic. Under walk, a reduction whose element type nothing fixes runs. The checker still needs it written, also for `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] f(j)`.
233	- `QQ` is exact. A negative shift count shifts the other way. `GCD` and `LCM` are never negative. `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits. `round` sends an exact half to the even integer.
234	- The library's numeral type is `IntLiteral`, a sibling that the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` convert from. Walk's numerals are unchanged for now.
235	
236	**Ranges.** Ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` or `ZZ` stops when built. A subscript of rank 2 or 3 is checked corner by corner, so a corner outside the bounds raises `IndexOutOfBounds`.
237	
238	### Arrays and the rest of the library
239	
240	- `fill` takes a value; `tabulate` takes a function.
241	- The array types bound their elements: `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`.
242	- An array's index type is bounded by `Index`, which only `ZZ32` of the integer types extends. Write `I extends Index` in your own generic over one.
243	- `String`'s juxtaposition, and each of `||`, `|||`, `//` and `///`, is three top-level operators.
244	- On the checker, a list of `RR64` or `QQ` has no `<`.
245	- Array storage is still boxed.
246	
247	### Walk
248	
249	- Walk converts by coercion at calls, bindings and assignments, picking the coercion from the run-time value.
250	- Walk infers type arguments through coercions. A type parameter nothing fixes takes its bound, and one whose bound names itself stays open.
251	- Walk chooses between a generic and a plain declaration by declared types, not by order in the file.
252	- At load, walk refuses some programs it used to run: an object extending two closed traits without being listed; two functional methods with no declaration on their meet; an object that leaves an inherited abstract method without a body, as five of the team's demos did before they were respelled; an `override` that overrides nothing.
253	
254	### The checker
255	
256	- It checks `nat` and `int` size parameters, arithmetic in a size and a size known only at run time, and infers static arguments through coercions.
257	- Overloads may differ in static parameters. The return-type rule is checked for every instance. Two generic overloads are valid where their parameter types exclude each other as a whole, on both paths.
258	- The overloads of every operator are checked, the symbolic ones too.
259	- In a self-typed trait, `self` in a body is also of the implementing type, so `floor(self): I = self` needs no cast.
260	- An `extends` entry may hold only under a `where` condition, as a list's order does.
261	- It judges two functional methods for each type that provides both.
262	
263	### The code generator and the run time
264	
265	- A top-level `var` compiles, and `atomic` covers it.
266	- A numeral of exactly 32 or 64 bits keeps its value.
267	- A sized program compiles, loads and runs. Generic code dispatches correctly on four threads.
268	- An object with no `asString` prints its type name.
269	
270	**The specification.** Appendix I has 42 entries, each with the original text and the reason.
271	
272	### Size of the internal changes
273	
274	- 194 commits touched the code, library or specification: 28 before the tag, 21 of them toolchain; 166 after it.
275	- Lines added after the tag: walk 4.8K, checker 3.4K, code generator and run time 1.0K, specification 6.7K, tests 20.9K. The library gained 4.1K lines and lost 2.6K.
276	- The grammar is unchanged. The suites grew from about 1.4K and 382 tests to 2.1K and 683.
277	
278	Sources: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/fortress-changes-chronology.md` part A (to batch 10); `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md`; `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` F-258, F-263, F-276 to F-281, F-285; `Specification/appendices/changes.tex` at `2bff2fe23`; `explorations/reviews/batch-22-review.md` section 1 (the suites); `git diff --numstat 75cca6683 2bff2fe23`; `git log 75cca6683..2bff2fe23` over `ProjectFortress`, `Library`, `Specification`, `bin` and `build.xml`; `git diff a874948ac 2bff2fe23` over the grammar files.
279	
280	## 6. The original Fortress and the revival's resolutions
281	
282	### Custodians, not authors
283	
284	The first principle of the protocol the work follows reads: "We are custodians of their language, not its authors." It asks the revival to finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification and by the library's own practice. Every agent is bound by the same rules through the skill it loads.
285	
286	- No committed file claims credit for the revival.
287	- Where git doesn't record who wrote something, the authorship is rebuilt from the history. It's never guessed.
288	- Reasons go into commit messages and reports, not into the team's source comments.
289	- Every claim is checked against a primary source: the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output.
290	
291	None of the team's tests or demos was deleted, and 63 were edited, each for a reason on record. All 52 team demos run to their end under walk. A batch that breaks a demo also repairs it, where the repair is known.
292	
293	### The team left three sources that disagree
294	
295	The team left Fortress in three forms, with the type papers beside them:
296	
297	- the specification, the text that says what Fortress is;
298	- the interpreter (walk) and its library;
299	- the compiler and its own, smaller library.
300	
301	These disagree in places. The revival changes the team's Fortress for one of two reasons only: two of these sources contradict each other, or a program fails. It reconciles them. Where the team's later work, in the compiler's library or the type papers, departs from the original specification, the revival follows the later work. It then updates the specification to match what it implements. A callout marks the passage, and Appendix I keeps the original text with the reason.
302	
303	### Example: the number types
304	
305	- The team's interpreter library put the number types in a tower. A narrower type was a kind of the wider type: `ZZ32` was a kind of `ZZ64`, and `ZZ64` a kind of `ZZ`.
306	- The prelude went from siblings to a tower and back in 2009. Christine Flood declared its widths as sibling objects in March. Jan-Willem Maessen made them a tower later that month. David Chase cut the subtyping between the widths in August. Sukyoung Ryu added the first exclusion, `ZZ32 excludes ZZ64`, in October. Maessen and Eric Allen widened the exclusions and added the first coercions, from November 2009 to January 2010. Guy Steele built the comparisons and the integer operators on the flat prelude in 2011.
307	- In 2010 Justin Hilburn built the exclusion rule into the checker: no type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. In the tower, `ZZ32` is both an `Integral` of `ZZ32` and, through `ZZ64`, an `Integral` of `ZZ64`, which the rule refuses. The siblings obey it.
308	- On 09-24 the curator chose to keep the rule. Batch 6 made the interpreter's library siblings too, on 09-27, so that the checker accepts it.
309	
310	So a model that remembers the tower remembers the team's interpreter library correctly. What it doesn't know is that the team's compiler had left the tower in 2009.
311	
312	### Left as the team had it
313	
314	- Functional methods: a method with `self` among its parameters is called as `f(x)`.
315	- Juxtaposition as an operator, and the whitespace rules. The grammar is unchanged.
316	- Declarations: `x = e`, `var x: T = e`, `x := e`.
317	- Loops and reductions are library code. A `for` loop, a comprehension and `SUM` turn into calls to library objects: a generator, which produces the values, and a reduction, which combines them.
318	- Evaluation is parallel by default. The revival pins the suites to four threads in the build file.
319	- Only the compiled path checks static types. Walk checks more when it loads a program, but these aren't static types.
320	- What the specification describes and the team never built is still unbuilt: dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions, reduction variables, complex numbers.
321	
322	### Where the revival resolved a contradiction
323	
324	#### Dispatch on every argument
325	
326	- **Overloads that differ in static parameters.**
327	  - Original: one sentence of the Working Draft forbids this. The 1.0 release of March 2008 doesn't have it. In git, the sentence first appears in the specification's sources as Sukyoung Ryu re-imported them in November 2009. Neither implementation enforced it. The checker implements the type group's model of 2011, from their OOPSLA paper, which allows such overloads.
328	  - Resolution: such overloads are allowed, and the specification states the 2011 model. The implementations and the library already overload across static parameters, and enforcing the sentence would refuse about 180 pairs of declarations in the library's apis.
329	- **The return-type rule.**
330	  - Original: the 2011 paper asks for the rule on every instance of a generic declaration. The checker tested one. A pair that broke the rule then passed the checker and failed the JVM's check of the bytecode.
331	  - Resolution: the checker tests every instance, as the paper asks. Such a program now fails when it's compiled, not when it runs.
332	- **How walk chooses between a generic and a plain declaration.**
333	  - Original: the specification chooses by the declarations' types. Walk chose by their order in the file.
334	  - Resolution: walk now chooses by the declared types, as the specification says. A program's answer no longer depends on the order of its declarations.
335	- **Generic declarations that exclude each other only as a whole.** Both implementations refused such a pair. The 2011 paper accepts it, by reading the parameter types together. Both paths now follow the paper.
336	- **Symbolic operators.** The checker skipped their overloads. The team knew the gap: its appendix of proposed features calls the two subscript operators "not really a valid overloading". The checker now checks every operator.
337	
338	#### Traits and objects
339	
340	- **The exclusion rule.**
341	  - Original: the checker has enforced the rule since 2010, and the 2011 paper states it. The Working Draft doesn't, and some of its examples break it.
342	  - Resolution: the specification states the rule. It keeps the examples that break it, marked "Not allowed". Without the rule, the checker's return-type rule lets through programs that die with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`.
343	- **What a `comprises` clause says.**
344	  - Original: four passages of the Working Draft read it as a statement about types, and so are false for some programs it allows. The Types chapter of the 2012 restart reads it as a statement about values.
345	  - Resolution: every value of the closed trait is a value of a listed type. Read by values, the passages hold.
346	- **The vectors' algebra.** The team's vectors are additive groups, and its library also adds an array and a number. By the team's rules these overloads are valid together, but the checker could not show it. The library stays as the team wrote it, and the checker now reads the self type.
347	
348	#### Static parameters
349	
350	- **The bound of a type parameter with no written bound.**
351	  - Original: the Working Draft says `Object`. The library uses its generic containers with tuples, which `Object` doesn't hold, and writes `Any` where it states a bound.
352	  - Resolution: the bound is `Any`, because the library works only with `Any`.
353	- **A type parameter that nothing in a call fixes.**
354	  - Original: the implementations gave it the empty type `Bottom`, or left it unsolved, and some such compiled calls failed the JVM's check of the bytecode. The POPL 2019 paper of Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu gives such a parameter its bound, never `Bottom`.
355	  - Built: the specification states the paper's rule. The checker infers such a parameter at its bounds, never at `Bottom`. Walk gives it its declared bound, and leaves open one whose bound names itself, such as `SUM`'s. Walk still gives `Bottom` in three narrow cases.
356	  - Not built yet: at run time both implementations still run a dispatched generic declaration at the value's type where nothing fixes the parameter. The compiled path waits for phase 5, when its dispatcher will carry the call's static return type.
357	- **The index type of a subscript.** The team wanted an index bounded by an `Index` type that excludes the ranges, but `a[1, 2, 3]` passes a tuple, and they needed "a magic to convert that tuple argument expression to something of type Index". The bound is built, and a tuple of `Index` types is an `Index`. That tuple rule departs from the team's text on tuples, and the specification says so.
358	- **Sizes on the compiled path.** The specification has size parameters. The compiled path couldn't carry them, but its code generator had a slot reserved for them. The revival fills the reserved slot, in the team's pattern for type arguments, and a program with sizes now compiles and runs.
359	
360	#### Numbers
361	
362	- **Conversion in walk.** The specification says that a call converts its arguments when that makes it apply. Walk had a note "TODO add checks for COERCE" at that place. Walk now converts the arguments, doing the work the team's note left to do.
363	- **Overflow.** The specification and the compiled path raise `IntegerOverflow` when a fixed-width result doesn't fit; walk wrapped the result. Walk now raises it too. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's own wrapping operators.
364	- **Ranges.** The interpreter's ranges took any integer type, the prelude's only `ZZ32`. Ranges are now over `ZZ32` only, as in the prelude, since a JVM array index is a 32-bit integer.
365	- **The integer power.** The Working Draft gives it a rational value, which the team never built. The team's later code gives it its base's type, and the revival follows that code (part 5).
366	- **`SUM` and `PROD`.** `SUM` used catch-all operators on `Number`, which went with the tower. `SUM` and `PROD` are now one generic declaration each, over the element type's own algebra.
367	
368	### Where the quiz was right about the original
369	
370	A fresh model answered a quiz on Fortress from its training alone (part 4). The audit graded each answer against today's tree, so an answer can be right about the team's Fortress and still be graded down:
371	
372	- The quiz didn't say how the number types relate. A reader who assumes a tower, narrower below wider, describes the team's interpreter library exactly.
373	- Its answer that overflow raises an error, graded correct, holds for the team's specification and compiler. The team's walk wrapped.
374	
375	Some answers marked wrong come from the team's own specification, which describes more than the team built:
376	
377	- `Monoid[\T, ⊕\]` with laws: a chapter of the specification. The library has it only in a comment and in its incomplete folder.
378	- `fortress run Foo.fss`: the specification's overview says this. The team's tool runs a program under walk with `fortress Foo.fss`.
379	- Complex numbers: named in the specification, in no library.
380	- Tests that state their expected output: the team's compiler tests do this. Its interpreter tests don't.
381	
382	Two answers are wrong for both the team and the revival: integer types that wrap by themselves (the specification wraps only with its own operators), and an `Any` type that doesn't hold tuples. One more is wrong for the team: the guess that walk built part of the coercion rules. The team's walk had none.
383	
384	Sources: `explorations/protocol.md` (principle 1); `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md`; `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` and `POSITIONS.md` (the flattening, the exclusion rule, the static-parameter sentence, the instance rule; P-79, P-152, P-153, P-155 to P-157); FACTS F-283; `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/overloading.tex` lines 100 to 108; `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/spec-sentences-dated.md`; `git diff --diff-filter=M` and `=D a874948ac 2bff2fe23` over the team's test and demo folders; `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-existential-reduction/REPORT.md` (the pair refused on the base); `Papers/Types/exc-reduction.tick`; `Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex` lines 186 to 207; `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, "The index type of a subscript"; `explorations/reviews/type-decisions-review/judgement.md` V1, V2 and V10; `explorations/reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md`; `skills-distillation-audit.md` section B; the team's commits, read with `git show -s`: b2880c05c, 76c267f98, 6896886fb, 3e0306166, 128f313b5, 2ef730c88, d0cde7d17, b3c2e1342, da5291587, d535963cb (the prelude's numbers); 5a6b7913b, e828b44b1 (the exclusion rule in the checker); cec470a34, 0f49d8698 (the static-parameter sentence); 166841592, 275b90773 (the 2012 restart).

# Review of the revival page: text A and plan B

A is the current page text, and B is the proposed order. "Part N" and "line N" are in A. "Section N" is in B. An outsider is a reader who is not a member of the project.

## 1. A as a story, read fresh

**What A gives an outsider.**
- Part 6, "The team left three sources that disagree" (lines 293-301), tells why the revival changes the language.
- Part 6, "Example: the number types" (lines 303-310), shows that method on one case.
- Part 1 (lines 21-27) gives facts that a reader can check, such as 10.9 s against 22 ms for one training step.

**What A does not give an outsider.**
- A never says what Fortress is. Line 9 only names its designers.
- A never says who does the work. Only line 28 ("worker agents") and line 30 ("outside this session") show that AI models do it. A uses "curator" 22 times, from line 5, and never defines it.
- The rule ("custodians, not authors") comes at line 282. I read 280 lines before I knew why any change was made.

**Where I could not follow.**
- Part 2 is not in date order. The post-mortem of 09-29 (line 150) comes after batch 22 of 10-24 (line 141). Part 4 then goes back to 10-04.

# The revival page: a proposal for its new shape

Proposal for the curator, not done. "v20" is the text at `9556daf62`, which Professor Ryu received. "v24" is the text at `703d005d1`, the last publish. Both are `process-engineering/revival-story.md`. Sizes are in characters of the text. The drift note's hybrid (its section 8, option 2) is rejected and not used here.

## 1. The readers and the job

The page has two readers:

- A reader from outside the project who knows programming languages: among them the team's own designers, such as Professor Ryu, who know Fortress far better than the revival does, and readers who know only its name. The repository's README is about the language as the team left it. This page is about the revival.
- The curator, who reads it to close his gap on what happened since the tree was unsealed on 17 September.

Its one job: tell what the revival did and why, as a story in plain words, and where it stands now. It stays one page, kept current after each landing and each phase's close.

## 2. The story's order

The story comes first, then two reference parts. Each section ends with its references, by file and section.

1. **Opening** (0.4K). What Fortress was, with a link to the README; what the revival does; its measure, microGPT compiled to bytecode and running fast; the date of the last update. From v20's header. Cut: "for the curator", and the glossary up front, which moves to section 10.
2. **Where it stands** (0.8K, a fixed block). The phase and its aim; the last landing and its date; the checker count and the distance; microGPT under walk and on the compiled path; the next step. New. It replaces v24's "Batches 14 to 22", its token list, "Phase 3's end" and "Phase 4's first batch" (3.2K), status written as prose. Only the script writes it (section 3).
3. **What the revival is, and its rule** (2.2K). The team; the three sources that disagree; custodians, not authors; each change to the specification marked, with the original text in Appendix I. From v24 part 6, "Custodians, not authors" and "The team left three sources that disagree", moved to the front because every later part rests on them. It defines team, walk, compiled path, checker, the one library, the prelude and the switch-over. Its count of the team's edited tests moves to section 8.
4. **Running the 2012 tree again, 19 August to 16 September** (2.0K). The build on current Java; the microGPT ports, 10.9 s a training step against 22 ms in Python; the runs that hunted gaps; the gap ledger; the map; the sealed tree. From v20 part 1, cut from 2.8K: the run letters (B, B2, C to C4), the ledger's row counts per merge, row 148.
5. **How the work runs: phases and batches** (2.2K and the batches chart). The six phases; a batch in plain words, explained once, here; the gate; to land; the two numbers, and why they sometimes rose. The batches chart sits here, and the text explains how to read it. From v20 part 2, "How a batch works", "The plan" and "The checker's errors falling". Cut: the agents' role names (skeptic, judge, repair, gather, merged-diff review), the ladder, the batch names' suffixes in prose (3.5, 6b, 7R, N, 7C), and the lists of the count and the distance by batch (1.1K in v24, 37 lines), which become the chart.
6. **The phases so far** (4.5K now, at most 1.5K more a phase). One chapter for each phase, as synthesis: its aim, its decisions and why, what went wrong, its dates and its number of batches. Chapters: before the plan, 17 to 25 September (test first, one library); phases 1 and 2 (sizes at run time, overflow, the flat number tower); phase 3, 28 September to 30 October (the checker at zero, with the zero's readings in one sentence); phase 4 at its close. From the 19 "main decisions" of v24 part 2, regrouped by phase. Cut: the lines per batch, restarts, held pushes, open asks, "the curator's call", the batch number on each decision.
7. **How the record grew** (2.6K and the record chart). What the record is: the gap ledger, the facts, the decisions and the index of notes. The chart, and text on its shape and its jumps: the ledger's rewrite of 8 October, the consolidation of 13 October, the rewrite of 22 October after each decision was traced to the curator's own words, the scratch files of 29 September, and the written instructions that every agent loads. From v20 part 3 whole, v24 part 3's two added lines, and v20 part 4 cut to the lessons that explain the chart. Cut: the shared build, the 7.0M probe, the six priced designs, the context study, tool names, "A commit outside the batch", "No timing of walk", and the type-decisions review as an event (its finding stays in section 9). They are about tuning the agents. On 13 October he wrote "Nothing about improving the agentic coding has place here!", though v20 kept a short part 4.
8. **What changed for a programmer** (4.1K). v24 part 5 whole, by area, with Appendix I's count and the size of the changes.
9. **The team's sources and the resolutions** (8.2K). From v24 part 6: the number types as the example, "Left as the team had it", and the 17 resolved contradictions in four groups. Cut: "Where the quiz was right about the original" (1.4K), which grades a model's memory. Its two points for a reader fold in: the tower is the team's interpreter library, and the team's walk wrapped on overflow.
10. **Words used on this page** (1.0K). v20's glossary, at the end, for a reader who jumps in.

The whole: about 28K of text and 3K of references, 31K, against v20's 31.6K and v24's 41.0K.

**Terms that go, as internal lingo:** record handles (P-152, F-283); review-queue items; ledger row numbers; rung letters, and the word rung; the agents' role names; "climb batch" (say batch); the ladder; `XXX` test names; tool and workflow names (`ledger.py`, `spend.py`, the orientation and record-landing workflows); commit hashes in the prose (the references keep them). **Terms that stay**, each defined at its first use: batch, phase, gate, land, checker count, distance, walk, compiled path, checker, the one library, the prelude, switch-over, the sealed tree, gap ledger, record, curator.

## 3. Keeping it current on the same page

**At a landing, no prose.** A script replaces three things whole and touches nothing else:

- the "where it stands" block, between two marker comments in the text, filled from PLAN's "Where we stand" (its "Landed" and "Next" items) and the gate's `summary.txt`, `checker-count.txt` and `distance.txt`;
- the batches chart, from `record-growth/landings.csv` (the script adds the landing's row, today kept by hand) and each landing's gate files;
- the record chart, by `measure.py` and `chart.py`, as today.

The captions and the text around the charts hold no live numbers. The coordinator looks at the result, publishes by URL and commits the text and the two images. Cost: the script once, 0.15M to 0.3M tokens written (the record chart's scripts exist; the block and the batches chart are new); each landing, 0.02M to 0.05M.

**At a phase's close, one chapter.** The coordinator briefs one Opus writer with the diff of `revival-changes.md` since the last update, the phase's paragraph in PLAN or PLAN-history, Appendix I's new entries, and section 2 as its keep and leave-out lists. The writer adds the phase's chapter to section 6, the phase's language changes to section 8 and its new resolutions to section 9, and brings the sizes in sections 7 and 8 to the phase's close. A phase adds at most 2.5K; past a cap, the writer rewrites the part shorter. The coordinator checks the diff against the lists. The curator then reads it as a page, each changed section an item with the new words marked, before it lands. Then it is published by URL and committed. Cost: 0.25M to 0.5M a phase.

**Never at a landing, and not at a phase's close:** the earlier chapters, sections 3 and 4, and the resolutions already written. They change only at the curator's word.

**The first rebuild.** One Opus writer, from v20, v24 and this note, writes phase 3's chapter (batch 22c closed the phase on 30 October, PLAN "The phases") and brings sections 8 and 9 to phase 3's close; phase 4's changes wait for its close. The curator reads it as a page; it is published by URL to the same page and committed, so her link on `main` shows it. Cost: the writer 0.3M to 0.5M, his page 0.05M to 0.1M, and the script: about 0.5M to 0.9M in all.

## 4. The register

- Plain full sentences, for a reader who knows programming languages. Halfway to ASD-STE100: active voice, short sentences, one word for one thing. No fragments such as "after 7R: 10".
- No internal shorthand (section 2's list). Each project term defined at its first use.
- Numbers as K or M. Dates as "17 September".
- The team's people and papers named, as v20 names them.
- The synthesis kept: a chapter tells what happened and why, never one batch's results. A landing adds no prose and no copied results.

## 5. Open choices

1. **One chart or two.** Today's page has one chart, the record's growth; its named vertical lines are the batches.
   - (a) Keep that chart alone, and the two lists of numbers as text.
   - (b) Add a batches chart, drawn from those lists, which replaces them.
   - Recommendation: (b). The lists grew one line a landing; a chart that the script redraws keeps the prose fixed.
2. **What the batches chart and the block show after phase 3**, where the count and the distance stay at 0.
   - (a) The two numbers only.
   - (b) Also each phase's own measure: for phase 4, the library's Java bindings that only walk can call, 161 of 449 at batch 25 (PLAN, "Where we stand"). The gate does not write that count yet.
   - Recommendation: (b), with a gate stage that writes it.
3. **The tokens spent.**
   - (a) None.
   - (b) One total a phase in its chapter, and v20's lesson on the prompt cache in one sentence.
   - (c) Per batch, on the batches chart.
   - Recommendation: (b). An outsider asks what the work cost; a list per batch is how v22 drifted.
4. **The names of the agents' tiers.**
   - (a) Name Opus, Sonnet and Fable wherever the story says who did what.
   - (b) Name them once, in section 5, where a batch is explained, and say "an agent" elsewhere.
   - (c) No names.
   - Recommendation: (b).
5. **The resolutions.**
   - (a) One long part inside the story, after the phases.
   - (b) Behind the story, with section 8, as the order above has them; each phase's chapter names the resolutions it made in one line.
   - (c) Spread over the phases' chapters.
   - Recommendation: (b). 8K of resolutions in the middle stops the story for a listener, and her main interest stays whole in one place.

## Sources

- v20 and v24: `git show 9556daf62:` and `703d005d1:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/revival-story.md`; sizes counted per subsection.
- `postmortem-2026-10-28/revival-page-outlines.md`, sections 1 to 4; `revival-page-drift.md`, sections 4 to 8 (the costs of a writer and a script).
- His words: `HELD.md`, the line of 19:4x on 11-03; his messages of 10-10 06:27, 10-12 22:53 and 10-13 quoted in the drift note, section 2.
- The published page's files: one image, `record-growth.png` (Artifact listing, 11-03).
- `PLAN.md`, "Where we stand" and "The phases"; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-25/gate/`; `process-engineering/record-growth/README.md`, "Files".

Written at the gather stage of climb batch 22c (2026-10-30), the batch of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-22c.md` that closes phase 3 by the curator's framing (rungs O, B, L and A), on `main` from the base `c3c22817cba8d5a62523e2d7cb1ec19e474aaf84`. Every rung was approved: O, B and L by their skeptics with no contested fix, and A after a ruling, the judge upholding its skeptic's contested fix `eee518f60`. No rung had a repair round. Nothing was merged: each branch stays as it is, `wip/rung-export-operators` at `cb088d7d8`, `wip/rung-bound-any` at `20a8b8174`, `wip/rung-list-imports` at `4308fa586`, `wip/rung-abstract-declared` at `d051d8002`.

**Preconditions.** `git status --porcelain` printed nothing, and `c3c22817c` is an ancestor of `HEAD` (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`, exit 0). `main` was three commits past the base when the gather began (`16190b24f`, `e4ea7bcec`, `c49290093`), each adding evidence files under `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-10-28/` only (`git diff --stat c3c22817c c49290093`: '3 files changed, 730 insertions(+)'), and no other commit came to it while the gather worked.

**Scratch.** The patches are `tmp/gather/<slug>.patch` in the main tree, each `git diff c3c22817c...<branch>`. The rung commits were composed on `main` itself, each patch applied with `git apply --3way --index`, its record folded and its commit made before the next patch was applied. For the merged-tree tests a tree was seeded outside the main tree from the batch's base build: `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh /home/user/fortress-base23 /home/user/fortress-gather22c - c3c22817cba8d5a62523e2d7cb1ec19e474aaf84` ("seeded from /home/user/fortress-base23 (e0ec620a9) in 3 s"; `git diff --stat e0ec620a9 c3c22817c -- Library ProjectFortress build.xml bin Specification` prints nothing, so the base build's code is the base's). There the four patches were applied together, in the order below, with `git apply --3way --index` (no conflict), and since rungs O, L and A edit the checker's Scala and rung B `Shell.java`, the tree was built (`ant compileAll`: 'Caches /home/user/fortress-gather22c/default_repository/caches started again, empty', 'BUILD SUCCESSFUL') and the library order run ('rc LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss 0' ... 'rc ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss 0', the five jars listed). Nothing was built or run in the main tree or in the base build. The code and tests the merged-tree tests ran on are `main`'s: the gather tree's index written as a tree (`git write-tree`, `811d7f717`) against `main` after the four rung commits, `git diff --stat 811d7f717 cc47b637d -- Library ProjectFortress Specification build.xml bin explorations/coordinator/tools`, lists only `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java` and `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala`, a comment line each that the gather corrected (below), and `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, the row number and the Effect sentences the gather wrote (below).

- P-27 **What a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library, in the library's own way.** A program written on this library has a part that states its algorithm, and it can have a part that builds domain-independent machinery that the library lacks, as both microGPT programs do. A form of that second part goes into the standard library when, on reasonable judgment, it is not an extension of the program's own domain; a form that the library has for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks for another is the plainest case. Whoever writes it there first studies how the library does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern, such as its `excludes` clauses. This rule governs how the library is extended; it does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language (P-26).
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.
- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. The minute is the curator's goal, for a check that runs only about two forward-and-backward passes of the model, not a full training, and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. The commit stage of each batch, the step that lands its changes, runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.
- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. `INDEX.md` is read whole at the coordinator's boot, at the start of each session and after each compaction, and each worker's brief carries a mission briefing from the territory map, not the whole map. The territory map's surveys date from 2026-09-16 (its README), so a status or a line number in them can be stale.
- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3 ends when the compiled checker reports no error on the apis and components of the interpreter's library that the distance to the switch-over counts (F-53 defines the distance, says what it counts and holds its value). The library's other components are not part of phase 3: each is cleared before the first program that needs it, and at the latest before walk runs the checker (P-12), so `System` by the switch-over, since the compiler's tests need it (F-293); F-290 counts their errors. Phase 4, the switch-over: first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.

### The one library and the compiled checker

- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.
- P-38 **The compiler prelude's own text is not repaired: its defects go with it at the switch-over.** A helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is fixed for the one library, and the prelude's value moves with it (F-313). Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on.
- P-39 **Every batch's gate measures the checker count, and its total never turns the gate red.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. Its gate runs the gate's steps on their merged tree, and then the checker count, as step 8 (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`); the gate of `fortress-repo`'s gate part has no such step. The checker count and the distance to the switch-over both count the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library. The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error that it cannot get past; the distance counts every error, over all apis and components (F-53 defines both and holds their values). A rise of the count's total is reported and never fails a batch on its own. The count's stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names. One is a checker crash that no rung of the batch listed in advance as expected, in the field `expectedCheckerCrash` of the batch's manifest, the part of the batch's script that declares each rung's task. Until the switch-over lands, every batch's gate also measures the distance, in a stage that only reports. Why: the count checks only the `FortressLibrary` component (F-53), so a native binding moved onto a helper in another component is checked by the distance alone, and P-58 has each moved binding checked from the step that moves it.
- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array dies with a raw Java exception (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).
- P-41 **On the compiled path, a size static argument travels at run time as a descriptor object, as a type argument does.** A generic type's descriptor has a field for each of its static parameters that is not an operator. The team's code generator already emitted that field for a size, with nothing to put in it, and the size's descriptor fills it. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor, which `RTTIsize.of` takes from a table; no Java class is written for it. This is the team's pattern for instantiating types, applied to numbers. An operator static argument, by contrast, stays a name known only at compile time (F-39, how both paths carry it). The curator sees no need for an operator argument to be carried at run time the way types and sizes are. F-129 holds what runs and its open rows.
- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`.
- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.

51:- F-54 **The gate classes the distance to the switch-over by root cause.** The `#class` rows of each gate's `distance.txt` hold the count of each class, such as X1 for an export error, BR for a big operator's body, and OT for the other body errors, one-off library slips and checker limits; `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/classify.py` assigns them. F-53 gives the last gate's. That gate's `distance.txt` reads `#crash none`: the checker checks the `FortressLibrary` component to its end, `Array3`'s body included, without a crash (F-233). Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/distance-triage.md` section 2.
63:- F-66 **The checker-count stage's table, `gate/checker-count.txt`, lands with every batch beside the gate's `summary.txt`.** Its total at the last landed gate is F-53's count. Step 8 of a batch's gate compares it with the newest landed table. The total is never red on its own, as P-39 rules, since a fix can raise it and the effects of two rungs on it do not add up. The gate is red on a crash line that no rung declared in its manifest (`expectedCheckerCrash`), on a table with no total, and on a stale shadow: the instrumented copy of `StaticChecker` beside the stage (`checker-count/shadow-src/`), when the tracked `StaticChecker` no longer matches the checksum that `run.sh` records. Detail: `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, "The checker count, and a rung whose test is that stage".
99:- F-233 **The compiled checker types a block's local functions with their group in scope.** So a local function with no written return type whose body calls another member of its group, as `Array3`'s `asString` does, checks; one that calls itself is refused for its reference cycle, as a top-level function is. Gated by `compiler_tests/LocalFunctionSiblingInLoop`, `LocalFunctionSiblingCall` and `XXXLocalFunctionRecursiveUntypedReturn`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-bounds/REPORT.md` section 6.
125:- F-288 **The fourteen components the distance checks are closed under import, and the compiled checker passes all of them.** `List` imports `CovariantCollection` and `OneShotFlag` (`Library/List.fss:13`, `:15`). Both are in the distance stage's list (`tools/distance/run.sh:87-90`), and both import nothing. Over the fourteen, the stage reads '#total 0', '#crash none'. `CovariantCollection`'s api states its component's members and headers, and its `upward` takes its target type from its first argument. The export check matches an object's value parameter by its modifiers other than `var` and its type, not by its name (row 839). Every `ArrayList` holds `OneShot` fields (`List.fss:253-254`) and every list comprehension goes through `covariantCompr` (`List.fss:178-179`), so after the switch-over `List` compiles only with both (the distance measures the checker, not the code generator). Tests: the distance stage; `compiler_tests/ExportVarObjectParameter`; `tests/CovariantCollectionArmsWalk.fss` for walk's values. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-list-imports/REPORT.md`, sections 1 to 3.

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's distance stage: the compiled checker over the whole interpreter library, the
# fourteen components, the prelude's twelve and the two that List imports, and their apis,
# every stage of every unit run whatever the earlier stages reported, so that nothing hides
# behind an early return; one table.
#
# Why it exists: Pavol's answer 11 (POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-26): the full measurement of the
# distance to the switch-over "becomes a report-only stage of phase 3's gates, whose job is
# driving it down". The checker-count stage beside it (../checker-count/run.sh) sees only
# the errors before each api's early return, 62 of about 1,740 on 2026-09-27.
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched: the
# shadow sources and classes, the driver, the checker's caches (-Dfortress.caches) and the
# JVM's temporary directory (so Rats! leaves nothing in /tmp) go to the scratch directory
# (default: $TMPDIR or /tmp), and the caches are deleted at the end. It never removes
# /tmp/fortress*rats, which other runs on the machine use. Exit 0 if the table was
# produced, 1 if it could not be. One JVM, -Xmx4g, one busy core: 789 s on the idle 4-CPU
# container on 2026-09-27, 14 to 24 minutes under load 7 to 18 (switch-over-distance-flat.md
# section 5); the table's #seconds and #machine rows say what each run took and where.
#
# The setting: "compile" by default, the compile command's own: DistanceMulti's -setting
# compile takes the extends-Object pre-desugaring from the line that opens
# Shell.useCompilerLibraries() in the tracked ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java,
# read at each run (the run stops, with no total, if that line is not there; its "### order="
# line prints the switch it read, extendsObject=...), and turns the compiled-expression
# desugaring on, as the compile path does. Answer 11 names the compile path's setting. That
# line sets the switch off, the implicit bound Any of P-42 (row 412), so the default runs as
# "any", which fixes the switch off whatever Shell.java says; with the switch on, the compile
# setting gave 685 errors on climb batch 22's code, 580 on the bound Object (F-289). "any"
# differs from walk's setting by the compiled-expression desugaring: on the tree of 2026-09-27
# 1,746 to 1,747 errors against 1,737 to 1,738 (FACTS.md, "The true distance to the
# switch-over"). The third argument, any or walk, runs another setting, for a comparison
# with the measurements on file; the gate never passes it.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false), as in
# every run of the measurement: keyed on declaration pairs, it hides 27 to 35 errors
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/distance"
SCRATCH=${2:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/distance.$$}
case "$SCRATCH" in /*) ;; *) SCRATCH="$PWD/$SCRATCH" ;; esac
SETTING=${3:-compile}
case "$SETTING" in any|walk|compile) ;; *) echo "distance: unknown setting $SETTING" >&2 ; exit 1 ;; esac
FLAGS="-Dprobe.tolerant=true -Dprobe.all=true -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false"
COMPONENTS="Library/FortressLibrary.fss Library/RangeInternals.fss ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss
 ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss Library/List.fss Library/String.fss Library/FlatString.fss Library/Stream.fss
 ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fss Library/TypeProxy.fss Library/Writer.fss ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss
 Library/CovariantCollection.fss Library/OneShotFlag.fss"

rm -rf "$SCRATCH/shadow-src" "$SCRATCH/shadow-classes" "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$SCRATCH/tmp"
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH/shadow-src" "$SCRATCH/shadow-classes" "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$SCRATCH/tmp" \
         "$(dirname "$OUT")" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | sed 's#:[^:]*/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache##')
#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table holds a total; 1 if no table could be produced, or if the table holds
# no total because the run's errors are not the checker's (#stopped, below). 20 s in the
# main tree, measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The run stops after the type checker (WorldFlip -stop check), since 2026-10-24 (climb batch
# 22): the compiler's own phase order up to and including TYPECHECK, integer literal folding
# included, as the distance stage's DistanceMulti -order check. Past the checker, the code
# generator's refusals are not the checker's errors (FACTS F-34 counts them), and its first
# one throws, so a run on a library the checker passes went on into the code generator and
# printed no total. A run the checker stops runs the same phases as before; a clean check,
# a run that reached the component's check and ended rc 0 with no error line, reads as 0.
#

Steele Jr.** and **Eric Allen** and developed from 2003 to 2012. The press framed its ambition as doing *"for Fortran what Java did for C"*; the project's own tagline was simpler — **"Simple parallelism, beautiful code."** In practice it became something broader — a laboratory for programming-language ideas that mainstream languages have been absorbing ever since: - **A growable language.** Following Steele's "Growing a Language" (OOPSLA 1998), almost everything — operators, loops, even the parallel machinery behind `∑` — is defined in libraries, not the compiler. - **A mathematical language.** Syntax modeled on whiteboard mathematics: Unicode operators (`∈`, `⊆`, `⌊x⌋`, `∑`), juxtaposition as a user-definable operator (`3 sin pi x`), nontransitive operator precedence (`a+b ∨ c+d` is rejected rather than misparsed), and comments that render as wiki markup. - **A parallel language.** Loops, tuples, argument evaluation, and big reduction operators are implicitly parallel; a work-stealing runtime balances the load ("do for processors what GC does for memory"); `atomic` blocks are backed by transactional memory. - **Traits, multiple inheritance, and symmetric multimethod dispatch**, with overloading checked by the Meet Rule — plus algebraic traits (`Monoid`, `Ring`, …) and design-by-contract woven into the type system. It looked like this — the heart of [`buffons.fss`](ProjectFortress/demos/buffons.fss), one of the original Sun Labs demos, estimating π by Buffon's needle. The `for` loop runs its iterations in parallel, `atomic` guards the shared counters, juxtaposition multiplies, and `0.0 < rsq < 1.0` is a chained comparison: Fortress code was meant to be read as mathematics. The rendering above is the canonical one, produced by [Fortify](Fortify/) — the project's own Emacs-and-LaTeX typesetter, the tool behind the specification and Steele's slides — from the ASCII source you actually type, where `delta_X` is δ_X, `SQRT` is the radical, and `|/ … \|` and `|\ … /|` are ⌈ ⌉ and ⌊ ⌋: ``` for i <- 1#3000 do delta_X = random(2.0) - 1.0 delta_Y = random(2.0) - 1.0 rsq = delta_X^2 + delta_Y^2 if 0.0 < rsq < 1.0 then y1 = tableHeight random(1.0) y2 = y1 + needleLength (delta_Y / SQRT rsq) (y_L, y_H) = (y1 MIN y2, y1 MAX y2) temp1:RR64 = y_L / needleLength temp2:RR64 = y_H / needleLength if |/ temp1 \| = |\ temp2 /| then atomic do hits:= hits + 1.0 end end atomic do n:= n + 1.0 end end end ``` 170:- [`explorations/`](explorations/), [`research/`](research/) — revival-era: 239:August 2012 wind-down; everything after that is the revival's own work

([US 8,843,887](https://patents.google.com/patent/US8843887B2/en) and
siblings) on 31 August 2012, the same day as the original repository's
[last commits](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/commit/a874948acb5b4b6aa7791e8d735657437910d879).

## Repository tour

The top level:

- [`ProjectFortress/`](ProjectFortress/) — the toolchain: all Java/Scala
  source under `src/com/sun/fortress/`, the `.fss` test corpora, and
  vendored third-party jars. Built by the root [`build.xml`](build.xml)
  (the one inside `ProjectFortress/` is a deprecation stub).
- [`Library/`](Library/) — the standard library, written in Fortress itself
  as `.fss`/`.fsi` component pairs; `FortressLibrary.fss` is the prelude.
  [`CompilerLibrary/`](CompilerLibrary/) holds API stubs for the compiler
  path.
- [`bin/`](bin/) — the `fortress` launcher and its supporting scripts.
- [`Specification/`](Specification/), [`Papers/`](Papers/),
  [`Documentation/`](Documentation/) — the research record, plus
  [`Fortify/`](Fortify/), the Emacs-based renderer that typesets Fortress
  source as LaTeX math for those documents.
- [`explorations/`](explorations/), [`research/`](research/) — revival-era:
  verified experiments and the authorship map.
- [`README.txt`](README.txt) — Sun's original SVN-era repository guide.

Inside [`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/),
the shape of the implementation:

- [`Shell.java`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java) — the CLI
  entry point, dispatching `walk` (interpret), `compile`, `run`, `parse`,
  `typecheck`, and friends.
- [`parser/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/) — four
  Rats!-generated packrat parsers (the main grammar plus a preparser,
  template parser, and import collector), with hand-written precedence and
  layout support in
  [`parser_util/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser_util/) and
  the extensible-syntax machinery in
  [`syntax_abstractions/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/syntax_abstractions/).
- [`nodes/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes/) — the generated
  AST classes, produced (along with Scala and Fortress mirrors of the AST)
  from [`ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`](ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast).
  Generated code is committed; `ant makeAST` regenerates.
- [`scala_src/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/) — the
  type checker, rewritten in Scala beginning in late 2008 (remains of the
  older Java checker sit in
  [`compiler/typechecker/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/typechecker/)).
- [`compiler/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/) —
  disambiguation, desugaring, and the JVM bytecode backend
  ([`codegen/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/),
  [`asmbytecodeoptimizer/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/asmbytecodeoptimizer/));
  its [`WellKnownNames.java`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/WellKnownNames.java)
  is the switch that gives the interpreter and compiler paths their
  different preludes.
- [`interpreter/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/) — the
  tree-walking reference evaluator, with native primitives in
  [`glue/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/).
- [`runtimeSystem/`](ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/) —
  the work-stealing runtime, and the class-load-time instantiation of
  generics that compiled code links against.

## Building, walking and running

Fortress needs only a JDK and Apache Ant; the build has been kept working
on modern JDKs.

```bash
export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/jdk
export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH
export FORTRESS_HOME=$(pwd)                    # repo root
ant compileAll
./bin/fortress ProjectFortress/demos/buffons.fss
```

That last command *walks* — the interpreter's own term for direct
evaluation — the Buffon's-needle demo excerpted at the top of this README.

There is also a partial JVM bytecode compiler (`fortress compile`, then
`fortress run`); it is incomplete — some constructs were never implemented
— but what exists works. The interpreter requires the filename (without
`.fss`) to match the component name, and the compiler path needs imported
library components compiled into its cache first.

To run the test suite: `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`.

## Lineage and license

This repository is a 2018 GitHub fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git
conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its history runs
from the January 2007 opening of the original `projectfortress.sun.com`
Subversion repository (moved to Mercurial on java.net in March 2011) to the
August 2012 wind-down; everything after that is the revival's own work
(2026). The lineage is set out in
[`explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`](explorations/coordinator/lineage.md).

Most of the code is the work of a small core — Sukyoung Ryu on the front
end from parser to type checker, David Chase on the compiler and runtime,
Jan-Willem Maessen on the standard library, Christine Flood on
transactions and the work-stealing runtime — with a wider circle of
students, interns, and visitors around them; the map of who wrote what,
reconstructed from the history, is in
[`research/authorship.md`](research/authorship.md).

Fortress is BSD-licensed, with third-party exceptions noted in
[`LICENSE`](LICENSE).
